extracted.intended_audience: researchers, department chairs, funding agencies, journal editors, and institutional leaders involved in research assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and best-practice recommendations for assessing the quality and impact of research outputs and for making hiring, promotion, and funding decisions that avoid reliance on Journal Impact Factors. Includes departmental hiring process suggestions, metric alternatives, and community responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use journal-based metrics (Journal Impact Factor) as a surrogate
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use journal-based metrics, such as Journal Impact Factors, as a surrogate measure of the quality of individual research articles, to assess an individual scientist’s contributions, or in hiring, promotion, or funding decisions. (DORA general recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JIF was developed for librarians to help with journal subscriptions and reports the mean citations per paper over two years; the mean is statistically flawed for highly skewed citation distributions. Using JIF as a proxy drives unhealthy competition, delays publication, can encourage overinterpretation or fraud, and harms career progression of early-career researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize scientific content over publication metrics or journal identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific content of a paper is much more important than publication metrics or the identity of the journal in which it was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors (review panels, hiring committees, funders) should focus on the scientific content of papers rather than venue; author notes that several funding organizations and review panels now focus exclusively on scientific content when making decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow and evaluate selected, annotated bibliographies from applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding organizations and institutions should allow researchers to articulate the significance of their own work through selected and annotated bibliographies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several funders (EMBO, Wellcome Trust, NIH, NSF, etc.) have instituted or strengthened guidelines permitting applicants to highlight and contextualize key contributions rather than listing venue-based metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and use article-level and field-independent metrics (with transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop alternative metrics that operate at the article level and are field-independent to provide more accurate and transparent approaches to research assessment (e.g., Relative Citation Ratio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New metrics (Hutchins et al. RCR and others) and tools can better measure article influence; they should be transparent and interpretable. However, the article notes limitations of article-level metrics, especially for evaluating early-career researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should provide article-level and field-specific metrics and consider removing JIF display
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should provide article-level and field-specific metrics accessible to authors and assessors and some journals should distance themselves from displaying Journal Impact Factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many journals now provide metrics on immediate attention and field-specific context; some journals (Molecular Biology of the Cell, Science, PLoS, eLife, AMS journals) no longer display JIFs on their websites to discourage JIF-focused assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and value preprints in assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage and accept preprints (e.g., bioRxiv) as part of research communication and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprints enable rapid communication and are increasingly accepted by journals; the author reports using bioRxiv preprints positively in hiring, funding, and tenure-related evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise departmental hiring materials to require articulation of contributions and vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Require candidates to clearly articulate the value of their past contributions and their future research vision in a brief cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asking for this helps assess candidate fit and potential for success in the specific departmental environment rather than relying on publication venue or pedigree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use open faculty review systems and low-barrier interview invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Enable broad faculty participation in application review (e.g., AcademicJobs) and invite candidates for initial interviews if any faculty member expresses interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open access to applications lets the whole faculty view and express interest; inviting Skype interviews when at least one faculty member is interested increases the candidate pool and diversity and reduces reliance on closed-door consensus committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use focused initial interview questions about research trajectory and fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask candidates specific, advance-notified questions about where their research program will be in five years and how the institution can help them get there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide questions ahead of time so candidates can prepare; 30-minute Skype interviews with a few faculty members help reveal vision and fit efficiently and fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request and evaluate a small set of representative papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask candidates to choose three representative papers for circulation among faculty as part of application evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining representative papers provides concrete evidence of the candidate’s scientific contributions beyond journal titles or impact factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate candidates on ability to ask important questions and pursue them (cumulative impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess future success by a candidate’s ability to articulate important questions and their demonstrated persistence in pursuing answers; value a series of solid advances across career stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research statement, seminar, chalk talk, and a track record of multiple solid papers (published in rigorous, field-specific journals) are better predictors of success than isolated high-impact publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage monetary or evaluative rewards tied to journal impact factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject practices that provide monetary awards based on journal impact factors or that arbitrarily ascribe zero value to research published in lower-impact journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such incentives distort scientific priorities and harm fair assessment; academic leaders should oppose these country- or institution-level practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentor trainees to communicate timely and build cumulative reputations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentors should encourage timely communication of results and building a reputation through a track record of completed projects rather than waiting for a single definitive 'home run' paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Packaging an entire thesis or multi-year project into a single paper delays training, reduces opportunities to learn writing and publishing skills, and may hinder career progression for trainees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community responsibility to question methods and advocate for sound assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the research community—mentors, chairs, review panelists, policy makers, students—must continually question assessment methods, advocate for sound decision-making, protest malpractice, and commit to accurate research assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress depends on collective action by both those who are judged and those who judge; education and advocacy are necessary to change entrenched practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use citation-distribution analyses rather than journal means to understand impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that citation distributions for papers in a journal are highly skewed/exponential, making the mean (JIF) an unreliable summary of individual paper impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical analyses (Larivière et al., KS tests) show wide variation within journals; assessment should consider distributions and article-level data instead of relying on journal averages.
